A Uniform Framework for Handling Position Constraints in String Solving (Technical Report)
Yu-Fang Chen, Vojtěch Havlena, Michal Hečko, Lukáš Holík, Ondřej Lengál

Abstract
. We introduce a novel decision procedure for solving the class of position string constraints , which includes string disequalities, ¬ 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝑖𝑥𝑜𝑓 \neg\mathit{prefixof} , ¬ 𝑠𝑢𝑓𝑓𝑖𝑥𝑜𝑓 \neg\mathit{suffixof} , 𝑠𝑡𝑟 . 𝑎𝑡 \mathit{str.at} , and ¬ 𝑠𝑡𝑟 . 𝑎𝑡 \neg\mathit{str.at} . These constraints are generated frequently in almost any application of string constraint solving. Our procedure avoids expensive encoding of the constraints to word equations and, instead, reduces the problem to checking conflicts on positions satisfying an integer constraint obtained from the Parikh image of a polynomial-sized finite automaton with a special structure. By the reduction to counting, solving position constraints becomes NP -complete and for some cases even falls into PTime . This is much cheaper than the previously used techniques, which either used reductions generating word equations and length constraints (for which modern string solvers use exponential-space algorithms) or incomplete techniques. Our method is relevant especially for automata-based string solvers, which have recently achieved the best results in terms of practical efficiency, generality, and completeness guarantees. This work allows them to excel also on position constraints, which used to be their weakness. Besides the efficiency gains, we show that our framework may be extended to solve a large fragment of ¬ 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑠 \neg\mathit{contains} (in NExpTime ), for which decidability has been long open, and gives a hope to solve the general problem. Our implementation of the technique within the Z3-Noodler solver significantly improves its performance on position constraints.

1.
Introduction

Solving string constraints (string solving) has been motivated initially
by the analysis of string manipulations in programs,
especially in preventing security risks such as cross-site scripting or SQL injection in web-applications.
In the last two decades,
the lively research community has managed to develop a number of string constraints solvers (overviewed in
Sec.

9
) that may be capable of realizing this goal.
String constraints solvers are being integrated within
SMT solvers such as
Z3
,
cvc
4/5, or
Princess
(
Rümmer, 2008
;
Liang et al., 2014a
;
Barbosa et al., 2022
;
de Moura and Bjørner, 2008a
)
, and the string
category has been introduced in the SMT competition
(
smt, 2024a
)
.
Since string solving is ubiquitous and string constraint logics are general,
string solving keeps finding also new applications,
such as analysing Simulink models
(
Ishii et al., 2022
)
, verifying UML models
(
Jha et al., 2023
)
,
or checking cloud access policies at Amazon Web Services
(
Rungta, 2022
)
.

The competition of string-solving methods is lively. While it was long dominated by the strongest industrial grade SMT-solvers
Z3
and
cvc
4/5, the leading positions have been recently taken by approaches based on finite automata. They include
Z3-Noodler

(
Chen et al., 2024
)
,
a recent winner of string categories of SMT-COMP
(
smt, 2024b
)
,

OSTRICH

(
Chen et al., 2022
;
Chen et al., 2019
)
, which supports the richest palette of string constraints with strong completeness guarantees,
Z3str3RE

(
Berzish et al., 2021
;
Berzish et al., 2023
)
, and loosely also one of the engines of
Z3

(
Stanford et al., 2021
)
.
Automata-based solvers excel especially in handling complex regular constraints with word equations and related constraints, such as transducer constraints or ReplaceAll.

Position constraints.

In this paper, we aim at remedying a weakness of automata-based techniques,
which is handling a class of constraints that we call
position constraints
.
The so-called
existential
position constraints can be reduced to checking disequality
of letters at two specific positions in strings (called a
mismatch
),
where the positions are determined through measuring lengths of certain
sub-strings—i.e., counting their letters and comparing the counts.
The prime example of such constraints are string disequalities (negated word
equations) like
xyx\neq yxz
, which can be reduced to the existence of
mismatching positions in the two strings that are at the same distance from the
strings’ start.
1
1

1

On a high-level, we might write such a formula as
\exists i\in\mathbb{N}\colon i\leq\max(\mathit{len}(xyx),\mathit{len}(yxz))\land(xyx)[i]\neq(yxz)[i]
where
\mathit{len}
denotes the length of the corresponding string obtained by substituting into the variables and
t[i]
denotes the
i
-th position in the string given by the term
t
.

Other existential position constraints include
\neg\mathit{prefixof}
,
\neg\mathit{suffixof}
,

\mathit{str.at}
, and
\neg\mathit{str.at}
.
A special place among position constraints is occupied by
\neg\mathit{contains}(t_{x},t_{y})
where
t_{x}
and
t_{y}
are concatenations of variables, which does not
reduce to a simple existence of mismatching positions (i.e., it is not an existential
constraints), but is equivalent to a string formula with
quantifier
alternation
, much harder to solve than existential formulae.
Informally, the formula says that there exists a string assignment to variables
such that for the two strings
w_{x}
and
w_{y}
obtained by concatenating
assignments of the variables in
t_{x}
and
t_{y}
, it holds that for all
alignments of the start of
w_{x}
inside
w_{y}
, the letter at some position of

w_{x}
does not match the letter at the aligned position in
w_{y}
.
The formula falls into the
\forall\exists
fragment of the string theory, which is undecidable
(
Marchenkov, 1982
;
Durnev, 1995
)
;
the decidability of
\neg\mathit{contains}
is a known open problem
(
Abdulla et al., 2021
)
.
Solvers use heuristics that handle only very simple cases or rough approximations.

Position constraints are practically relevant, for instance, a disequality may be generated in symbolic execution
at every else-branch of a program that tests the equality of strings.
Some solvers
may be able to guess the right solution for satisfiable position constraints with ease (CVC5 excels in this),
but especially unsatisfiable position constraints may be much harder;
no current solver can handle them satisfactorily.

The automata-based approach particularly reduces position constraints into combinations of equations and length constraints. The work
(
Chen et al., 2023a
)
even shows a version of this reduction that allows one to freely add disequalities to one of the largest known decidable fragments of basic constraints (word equations, regular membership, and string length constraints), the
chain-free fragment

(
Abdulla et al., 2019
)
,
while preserving decidability.
However, since equations are expensive,
the price of the reduction may be very high.
Indeed, essentially all string solvers use exponential-space algorithms to deal with word equations,
including the automata-based ones, and the problem is opaque even in theory:
equations with regular memberships are in
PSpace

(
Plandowski, 1999
;
Jeż, 2016
)
,
but decidability of their combination with length
constraints is a long-standing open problem.

The gist of our approach to solving position constraints.

In contrast, the procedure we propose in this paper starts only
after

the rest of the constraint is solved—transformed into the
monadic
decomposition

(
Hague et al., 2020
;
Chen et al., 2019
;
Veanes et al., 2017
)
, i.e., a formula
obtained by transforming word equations into regular
constraints—and then solves
position constraints quickly and efficiently by other means.

The specific technical problem we are solving is therefore
satisfiability of Monadic-Position constraints
:

(MP)

Satisfiability of a quantifier-free conjunction of a monadic constraint (a conjunction of
regular membership constraints and linear integer arithmetic (LIA)
constraints over string lengths, a.k.a. length constraints) and a conjunction of
position constraints with string terms as parameters (e.g.,
xyx\neq yxy
,

\neg\mathit{contains}(xyx,yxy)
).

Monadic decomposition is at the heart of how automata-based solvers, such as
Z3-Noodler
and
OSTRICH
, solve string constraints.
The fact that position constraints can be ignored in this process is the main distinguishing feature of our approach and the key to its efficiency.
Translating the entire MP to a monadic constraint first, as automata-based solvers currently do,
takes
exponential
space,
while our algorithm runs in
NP
for existential position constraints

and in
PTime
for a single one
.

Moreover, our framework also allows to make a step towards showing decidability of MP with
\neg\mathit{contains}
.
Namely, it allows to translate
\neg\mathit{contains}(t,t^{\prime})
combined with a monadic constraint
to LIA with a nested universal quantifier
when the languages constraining variables in terms
t
and
t^{\prime}
are
flat

(expressible as a concatenation of a fixed number of parts, where every part is
an iteration of a single word).
The resulting quantified LIA formula can be solved by an off-the-shelf solver
(SMT-solvers seem to be capable of solving the obtained formulae efficiently).
To the best of our knowledge,
our algorithm is the first one for exact reasoning with
\neg\mathit{contains}
that is
complete for a large and interesting fragment of the problem.

The technical basis of our approach.

Technically, given a set of position constraints and automata-represented regular membership constraints in the monadic decomposition, our procedure derives a LIA constraint that relates positions of mismatches and lengths of the strings assigned to variables.
Repetition of variables, e.g.,
xyx\neq yxy
or
\neg\mathit{contains}(xyx,yxy)
, the main limiting factor of decidable fragments, is handled too:
The length of every variable is extracted from a single run of its automaton, and its contribution to a mismatch position in the string is counted with the multiplicity equal to the number of the occurrences of the variable that precede the mismatch position.
For a single existential position constraint, the LIA formula is constructed by taking the formula for the Parikh image of an automaton with a specific structure, enriched with constraints that enforce seeing a mismatch of symbols at at the proper positions.

The construction is more complex with multiple position constraints that share
variables. The straightforward approach would be to enumerate an exponential
number of cases corresponding to all orders of mismatches in the position
constraints.
E.g., for the constraint
D_{a}\land D_{b}\land D_{c}
, we would need to consider orders like

(D_{a}^{1},D_{a}^{2},D_{b}^{1},D_{b}^{2},D_{c}^{1},D_{c}^{2})
,

(D_{a}^{1},D_{b}^{1},D_{c}^{1},D_{a}^{2},D_{c}^{2},D_{b}^{2})
, etc., where
D_{x}^{i}
denotes the
i
-th mismatch in
D_{x}
.
The generated LIA formula would then be exponential (more precisely in

2^{\Theta(n\log n)}
) to the number of position constraints.
Our
NP
algorithm for MP depends on the discovery of an equivalent polynomial encoding.
The encoding combines the Parikh image of a polynomial-size automaton that generates any number of mismatch positions in any order with an additional arithmetic constraint that rules out the “wrong” orderings.

Moreover, we show that MP with a
single
existential position constraint is in
PTime
by a reduction to 0-reachability in a one-counter automaton
(
Alur and Cerný, 2011
;
Melski and Reps, 1997
)
.

Practical impact on performance.

Our experiments show that our framework substantially improves the speed and
effectiveness of the automata approach to string constraint solving whenever
position constraints are involved.
On position-heavy cases from our benchmark (obtained from symbolic executions
of large software projects), the string solver
Z3-Noodler
extended with our
decision procedure for position constraints is the fastest of all solvers and
has less timeouts than
cvc
5, the only other solver that handles
these benchmarks well.
The performance of
cvc
5 and the modified
Z3-Noodler
is orthogonal,
reflecting the large difference between the two approaches, and together they
solve all but 10 out of the
\sim
150,000 benchmarks.

Z3-Noodler
also demonstrates its ability to solve hard instances of

\neg\mathit{contains}
on an artificial benchmark made to test solvers on constraints
involving
\neg\mathit{contains}
, where all other solvers fail.

Summary of contributions.

Our contributions can be summarised as follows:

(1)

We propose a procedure for handling position constraints in the automata-based approach efficiently, without the need of including them into a procedure for monadic decomposition.

(2)

We show that MP is in
NP
for existential position constraints and
in
PTime
for a single one.
This contrasts with the exponential cost of monadic decomposition.

(3)

We propose the first algorithm for exact reasoning with
\neg\mathit{contains}
that is guaranteed to work on a large and interesting fragment of the problem,
namely, the MP where the regular languages restricting variables within the terms in the arguments of
\neg\mathit{contains}
are
flat
, and show that the problem is in
NExpTime
.

(4)

Experimental results show that our techniques significantly improve the performance of one of the fastest string solvers,
Z3-Noodler
, on position constraints.

Context of our work.

Our focus is on the basic constraints that must be handled by a universal
practical string solver: combinations of word equations, regular constraints,
and length constraints (as witnessed, e.g., by the SMT-COMP
benchmark
(
Preiner et al., 2024
)
).
Besides the
PSpace
-completeness of classical decidability of equations with
regular constraints by Makanin, Plandowski, and Jeż
(
Makanin, 1977
;
Plandowski, 1999
;
Jeż, 2016
)
, decidability of the
full basic logic is a long-standing open problem, and it is open even when
equations are quadratic, where only two occurrences of every variable are
allowed
(
Lin and Majumdar, 2021
)
.
The known undecidability results are concerned with extensions of this logic
with other than basic constraints (here called extended constraints), and are
thus only marginally relevant to our current work.
These fragments concern unrestricted ReplaceAll, transducer-defined relations,
string-integer conversions, and other extended
constraints
(
Chen et al., 2018
;
Chen et al., 2022
;
Chen et al., 2020a
;
Chen et al., 2019
;
Lin and Barceló, 2016
;
Day et al., 2018
;
Day et al., 2024
)
.
The approach that started at
(
Abdulla et al., 2014
)
led to a discovery of the
largest decidable fragment of the basic constraints, the chain-free
fragment
(
Abdulla et al., 2019
)
.
It generalizes the earlier acyclic fragment of
(
Lin and Barceló, 2016
)
and the larger
straight-line fragment of
(
Abdulla et al., 2014
)
.
The other solvers, especially
Z3
and
cvc
5, which use different approaches
usually revolving around the congruence closure
(
de Moura and Bjørner, 2007
)
, can handle
similar class of constraints in practice, but do not come with strong
theoretical guarantees.
Limited extensions of straight-line or chain-free logics with extended
constraints were shown decidable
in
(
Chen et al., 2018
;
Chen et al., 2022
;
Chen et al., 2020a
;
Chen et al., 2019
;
Lin and Barceló, 2016
;
Day et al., 2018
;
Day et al., 2024
)
.
The automata-based approach transforms equations and regular constraints to
a monadic decomposition (a disjunction of conjunctions of regular constraints
of at most doubly exponential size), which is in turn transformed to a LIA
formula and solved using a LIA solver.
The decidable fragments are all based on prohibiting forms of “
cyclic
dependencies
” of string variables in word equations, and range from

PSpace
-complete to
2-ExpSpace
, depending on the allowed extended
constraints.
The position constraints that we discuss here are in this framework normally
solved by a reduction to the basic constraints.
Essentially, after obtaining doubly exponential monadic decomposition of the
other basic constraints, the original approach needs to run the doubly
exponential space procedure to solve the position constraints.
Our work allows to replace the second
2-ExpSpace
phase by an

NP
-algorithm (or
NExpTime
for our fragment of
\neg\mathit{contains}
), or even by
a
PTime
one in the simplest case of one disequality.

2.
Preliminaries

We fix a finite non-empty
alphabet

\Gamma
.
A
word
or
string
over
\Gamma
is a (finite) sequence of symbols
w=a_{0}\ldots a_{n-1}

from
\Gamma
, its
length

|w|
is
n
, and the symbol at index
0\leq i<n
is denoted as
w[i]=a_{i}
.
We use
\epsilon
to denote the
empty word
and
\mathbin{\circ}
denotes string concatenation
(we sometimes omit the operator, i.e.,
a\mathbin{\circ}b=ab
).

\mathbb{N}
denotes the set of natural numbers
\{0,1,\ldots\}
.

A
nondeterministic finite automaton
(NFA) is a tuple

A=(Q,\Delta,I,F)
where

Q
is a finite set of
states
,

\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Gamma\times Q
is a
transition relation

with transitions denoted as
q\xrightarrow{a}p
for
q,p\in Q
and
a\in\Gamma
,
and
I,F\subseteq Q
are sets of
initial
and
final
states respectively.
A
run

\mathcal{R}
of
A
over a word
w=a_{1}\ldots a_{n}\in\Gamma^{*}
is
a sequence of transitions
q_{0}\xrightarrow{a_{1}}q_{1}\xrightarrow{a_{2}}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_{n}}q_{n}
s.t.
q_{0}\in I
and
\forall 1\leq i\leq n\colon q_{i-1}\xrightarrow{a_{i}}q_{i}\in\Delta
.
The run
\mathcal{R}
is
accepting
if
q_{n}\in F
, and the language of
A

is the set
L(A)=\{w\in\Gamma^{*}\mid\textrm{there exists an
accepting run of }A\textrm{ over }w\}
.
A language
L\subseteq\Gamma^{*}
is
regular
iff there exists an
NFA
A
such that
L=L(A)
.
We sometimes define regular languages using regular expressions with the
standard textbook notation.

Given a set
U
, let
{\#{}U}=\{{\#{}u}\mid u\in U\}
denote the set of elements obtained from
U
’s elements by prepending them with
\#
.
The
Parikh image
of a run
\mathcal{R}
, denoted as
\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}}
, is
a mapping
\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}}\colon{\#{}\Delta}\to\mathbb{N}

such that
\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}}({\#{}t})

denotes the number of occurrences of transition
t
in
\mathcal{R}
.
We say that
A
is
flat
2
2

2

We note that our notion of

flatness
differs from the one from
(
Abdulla et al., 2017a
)
and is similar
to the one from
(
Leroux and Sutre, 2005
)
.

if for every two runs
\mathcal{R}_{1}
and
\mathcal{R}_{2}
it holds that if

\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}_{1}}=\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}_{2}}
, then
\mathcal{R}_{1}=\mathcal{R}_{2}
.
Structurally, this means that flat automata have the form of
directed
acyclic graphs
(DAGs) connecting
simple
(i.e., non-nested)
loops
.
We say that a regular language
L
is flat iff there exists a flat NFA
A

s.t.
L=L(A)
.
For instance, the language
(ab)^{*}c((ab)^{*}+(ba)^{*})
is flat, while the
language
(a+b)^{*}
is not flat.

Let
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{I}
be the sets of
string
and
integer variables
. String formulae are of the form:

\displaystyle\varphi::={}~~

\displaystyle\varphi\land\varphi\mid\varphi\lor\varphi\mid\neg\varphi\mid\varphi_{\mathit{atom}}

\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathit{atom}}::={}~~

\displaystyle x_{s}\in L\mid t_{i}\leq t_{i}\mid t_{s}=t_{s}\mid x_{s}=\mathit{str.at}(t_{s},t_{i})\mid\mathit{prefixof}(t_{s},t_{s})\mid\mathit{suffixof}(t_{s},t_{s})\mid\mathit{contains}(t_{s},t_{s})

\displaystyle t_{s}::={}~~

\displaystyle x_{s}\mid t_{s}\mathbin{\circ}t_{s}

\displaystyle t_{i}::={}~~

\displaystyle x_{i}\mid k\mid\mathit{len}(x_{s})\mid t_{i}+t_{i}

where

\varphi_{\mathit{atom}}
is an atomic formula,

L
is a regular language (given by a regular expression or an NFA),

t_{s}
is a string term consisting of a concatenation of string
variables
x_{s}\in\mathbb{X}
3
3

3

A string literal
u\in\Gamma^{*}
can
be encoded by a new string variable
x_{u}
and a regular constraint
u\in L_{u}

for
L_{u}=\{u\}
.
, and

t_{i}
is an integer term composed of sums of integer variables
x_{i}
,
integers
k\in\mathbb{Z}
, and lengths of string variables
\mathit{len}(x_{s})
.

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle x_{s}\in L

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\nu(x_{s})\in L,

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle t_{i}\leq t_{i}^{\prime}

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\nu(t_{i})\leq\nu(t_{i}^{\prime}),

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle t_{s}=t_{s}^{\prime}

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\nu(t_{s})=\nu(t_{s}^{\prime}),

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle x_{s}=\mathit{str.at}(t_{s},t_{i})

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\nu(x_{s})=w_{s}[\nu(t_{i})]\land\nu(t_{s})=w_{s}&\text{if }\nu(t_{i})<|w_{s}|,\\
\nu(x_{s})=\epsilon&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle\mathit{prefixof}(t_{s},t_{s}^{\prime})

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\exists z_{p}\in\Gamma^{*}\colon\nu(t_{s})\mathbin{\circ}z_{p}=\nu(t_{s}^{\prime}),

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle\mathit{suffixof}(t_{s},t_{s}^{\prime})

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\exists z_{s}\in\Gamma^{*}\colon z_{s}\mathbin{\circ}\nu(t_{s})=\nu(t_{s}^{\prime}),\text{and}

\displaystyle\nu\models{}

\displaystyle\mathit{contains}(t_{s},t_{s}^{\prime})

\displaystyle{}\mathrel{\Leftrightarrow}{}

\displaystyle\exists z_{c},z_{c}^{\prime}\in\Gamma^{*}\colon z_{c}\mathbin{\circ}\nu(t_{s})\mathbin{\circ}z_{c}^{\prime}=\nu(t_{s}^{\prime}).

Semantics of atomic predicates for a variable assignment
\nu

The semantics of formulae is defined as follows.
A (variable)
assignment
is a mapping
\nu\colon(\mathbb{X}\to\Gamma^{*})\cup(\mathbb{I}\to\mathbb{Z})
and we lift
\nu
to string
terms
t_{s}
and integer terms
t_{i}
in the usual way (
t_{s}\mathbin{\circ}t_{s}
as string concatenation and
t_{i}+t_{i}
as integer
addition), with
\nu(\mathit{len}(x_{s}))
being interpreted as the length of
the string
\nu(x_{s})
.
Semantics of atomic predicates is given in
Fig.

1
.

When used within the DPLL(T) framework, it is sufficient to consider only conjunctions of atomic formulae and their negations.
A
normal form
of such formula is

\mathcal{E}\land\mathcal{R}\land\mathcal{I}\land\mathcal{P}

where

•

\mathcal{E}
is a conjunction of word equations
t_{s}=t_{s}
,

•

\mathcal{R}
is a conjunction of regular memberships

x_{s}\in L
4
4

4

A regular
non-membership
constraint can be
translated into a
membership
constraint for a complement language.

such that for every
x_{s}\in\mathbb{X}
, there is exactly one regular
membership constraint in
\mathcal{R}
(and we use
L(x_{s})
to denote it),

•

\mathcal{I}
is a conjunction of integer constraints
t_{i}\leq t_{i}
where
t_{i}
’s do not contain
\mathit{len}(t_{s})
terms, and

•

\mathcal{P}
is a conjunction of position constraints of the following form:

\displaystyle t_{s}\neq t_{s}\mid x_{i}=\mathit{len}(x_{s})\mid x_{s}=\mathit{str.at}(t_{s},t_{i})\mid{}

\displaystyle x_{s}\neq\mathit{str.at}(t_{s},t_{i})\mid{}

\displaystyle\neg\mathit{prefixof}(t_{s},t_{s})\mid\neg\mathit{suffixof}(t_{s},t_{s})\mid{}

\displaystyle\neg\mathit{contains}(t_{s},t_{s})

We transform a conjunction of literals into
the normal form in the following way:

(i)

We substitute every non-negated occurrence of the predicates

\mathit{prefixof}(u_{p},v_{p})
,
\mathit{suffixof}(u_{s},v_{s})
, and
\mathit{contains}(u_{c},v_{c})

with the word equations
v_{p}=u_{p}z_{p}
,
v_{s}=z_{s}u_{s}
, and
v_{s}=z_{c}u_{c}z^{\prime}_{c}
respectively for fresh string variables
z_{p}
,
z_{s}
,
z_{c}
, and

z^{\prime}_{c}
(note that we cannot do a similar thing for negated occurrences,
since we would need to introduce universal quantifiers for the

z
-variables).

(ii)

For every string variable
x
, we compute a single NFA that represents
all regular membership constraints for
x
.

We will use
|\mathcal{R}|
to denote the sum of numbers of states of all NFAs
used for encoding the
\mathcal{R}
constraint.

3.
Overview

Given a formula in the normal form
\mathcal{E}\land\mathcal{R}\land\mathcal{I}\land\mathcal{P}
in the considered fragment, the main idea of our
approach is the following (focusing on the
\mathcal{P}
part).
Other automata-based approaches usually try to get rid of the
predicates in
\mathcal{P}
by transforming them into word equations and
length constraints (e.g.
(
Chen et al., 2023a
;
Havlena et al., 2024a
;
Chen et al., 2020a
)
), thus making their
word equations potentially much harder to process.
Handling word equations is the
most demanding task in string solving, as the best known algorithms
for dealing with word equations work in

PSpace

(
Plandowski, 1999
;
Jeż, 2016
)
and are not practical
5
5

5

Existing string solvers usually deal with word equations by
incomplete algorithms that do not guarantee termination.
(and in the presence of length
constraints, the decidability of the problem is currently unknown).

In our approach,
we take care of the constraints
in
\mathcal{P}
only after the word equations in
\mathcal{E}
have been
processed and the obtained constraint
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
contains no more word equations.
This is achieved by the stabilization-based procedure introduced in
(
Chen et al., 2023a
)
, which transforms
\mathcal{E}\land\mathcal{R}\land\mathcal{I}

into a disjunction of constraints
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}^{\prime}
extended with
a substitution mapping variables from the original constraints to a concatenation of
fresh variables occurring in
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
and
\mathcal{I}^{\prime}
.
The transformation comes with the additional property that the resulting
constraint is a
monadic
decomposition

(
Hague et al., 2020
;
Chen et al., 2019
;
Veanes et al., 2017
)
, which means that each
choice of the fresh variable assignment given by
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
forms a solution
of the original system of equations (the substitution defines how to obtain
values of variables occurring in
\mathcal{E}
from the fresh variables)
6
6

6

Strictly speaking, we only need monadic decomposition on the variables that occur in position constraints.
.
Using the substitution
map, we can substitute variables in
\mathcal{P}
in order to obtain a position
constraint
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\wedge\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\wedge\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
.
Therefore, we will now focus on solving formulae of the form
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\wedge\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\wedge\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
, which is the main contribution of this paper.

The main idea of solving a formula of the form
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
is by transforming
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
into a LIA formula that is then added to
\mathcal{I}^{\prime}
to obtain
a (potentially quantified) LIA constraint
\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}
, which can be solved by
an off-the-shelf LIA solver.
The procedure for transforming
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
into a LIA
constraint is based on constructing a
tag automaton

A_{\mathit{tag}}
, which is
an NFA whose
transitions are extended with
tags
.
The tags do not affect the run of
A_{\mathit{tag}}
, but are used for counting
“
positions
” where something interesting happens, e.g., for a string
disequality
x\neq y
, we count the position
\ell
of a single character
mismatch
x[\ell]\neq y[\ell]
.

A_{\mathit{tag}}
is constructed from the regular constraints in
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
based on
the atomic predicates in
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
.

4.
Tag Automaton

In this section, we define
tag automata
(TAs) used in the later sections
for encoding position constraints.
We note that TAs are used just to simplify
notation; one could build the framework on top of NFAs or some counter model,
such as Parikh automata
(
Klaedtke and Rueß, 2003
)
, cost-enriched finite
automata
(
Chen et al., 2020a
)
, or simply vector addition systems with
states
(
Hopcroft and Pansiot, 1979
)
,
for the price of a more cumbersome notation.

Let
\mathbb{T}
be a set of
tags
.
A
tag automaton
(TA) over
\mathbb{T}
is a quadruple
T=(Q,\Delta,I,F)
, where
Q,I,F
are as for an NFA and the set of transitions
\Delta
is
\Delta\subseteq Q\times 2^{\mathbb{T}}\times Q
.
We use

for all
1\leq i\leq n
.

\mathcal{R}
is accepting if
q_{n}\in F
.
The Parikh image of
\mathcal{R}
,
\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}}
, is defined in the same way as for NFAs.
We may write
Q(T)
,
\Delta(T)
,
I(T)
, and
F(T)
to refer
to the components of a TA
T
.

For an NFA
A=(Q,\Delta,I,F)
and a variable
x
, we define the tag automaton

\mathsf{LenTag}_{x}(A)=(Q,\Delta^{\prime},I,F)
over a set of tags

of a TA
T
, denoted as

\mathit{PF}(T)
is a
linear integer arithmetic

(LIA) formula with free variables

{\#{}\delta}
corresponding to numbers of occurrences of transitions
\delta\in\Delta
.
Models of
\mathit{PF}(T)
are, therefore, assignments

\sigma\colon{\#{}\Delta}\to\mathbb{N}
such that

(1)

\sigma\models\mathit{PF}(T)\quad\text{iff there is an accepting run~$\mathcal{R}$ of~$T$
s.t.~$\mathit{PI}_{\mathcal{R}}=\sigma$}

Constructing
\mathit{PF}(T)
can be done in the usual
way
(
Janku and Turonová, 2019
)
(cf.
Appendix

A
).
We will also work with the
Parikh tag formula

\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(T)
,
which is a formula whose models are numbers of each tag seen on an accepting run
in
T
, constructed as

(2)

Note that in
\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(T)
, the free variables
are now also the counts of tags from
\mathbb{T}
and a model is an
assignment
\sigma^{\prime}\colon({\#{}\Delta}\cup{\#{}\mathbb{T}})\to\mathbb{N}
.

5.
Solving Disequalities

In this section, we will show how to solve a formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land\mathcal{P}
where
\mathcal{P}
only contains disequalities.
We will start from the simplest case (a single disequality with two different
variables), proceed to an arbitrary single disequality, and finish with a system
of disequalities.

5.1.
I: A Single Disequality of Two Variables

First, we consider the simplest case, i.e., when the position
constraint
\mathcal{P}
contains a single disequality

(3)

x\neq y,

where
x
and
y
are two different string variables whose values are restricted
to regular languages
L_{x}
and
L_{y}
.
The constraint is satisfiable iff there exist strings
w_{x}\in L_{x}
and
w_{y}\in L_{y}
such that they are either

(i)

of a different length or

(ii)

they are of the same length
\ell
and there exists a position
0\leq p<\ell
such that
w_{x}[p]\neq w_{y}[p]
.

We will show how to construct a tag automaton and, from it, a LIA formula
\varphi^{\mathrm{I}}

that is satisfiable iff the disequality is satisfiable.
We assume that we are given NFAs
A_{x}=(Q_{x},\Delta_{x},I_{x},F_{x})

and
A_{y}=(Q_{y},\Delta_{y},I_{y},F_{y})
such that
L(A_{x})=L_{x}

and
L(A_{x})=L_{y}
with
Q_{x}\cap Q_{y}=\emptyset
.
For this, we construct a TA
A^{\mathrm{I}}
.
Intuitively,
A^{\mathrm{I}}
is obtained by first concatenating
\mathsf{LenTag}_{x}(A_{x})
with
\mathsf{LenTag}_{y}(A_{y})
using an

\epsilon
-transition into a TA
A_{\circ}
.
One can see
A_{\circ}
as an encoding of all possible models of
x
and
y
w.r.t. only regular constraints
7
7

7

In fact, the order in which we do the concatenation
does not really matter—the main objective is to obtain a TA such that an
accepting run in it represents a model of regular constraints
.
Then, we take three copies of
A_{\circ}
and connect them together with transitions
that represent detected mismatches:
the first copy is used for tracking the run of
A_{x}
before the position of
the mismatch in
x
is encountered,
the second copy is used for tracking the rest of the run in
A_{x}
and the
first part of the run in
A_{y}
(before the mismatch in
A_{y}
), and
the last copy tracks the rest of the run in
A_{y}
.
Moreover, the automaton is enhanced with tags that keep track of the position
of the mismatch in
x
and in
y
and the values of the mismatched symbols.

5.1.1.
Tag Automaton Construction

Formally, let
A_{\circ}=(Q_{\mathbin{\circ}},\Delta_{\mathbin{\circ}},I_{\mathbin{\circ}},F_{\mathbin{\circ}})
be a TA over

\mathbb{T}_{\mathbin{\circ}}=\{\langle\textbf{{S}},a\rangle\mid a\in\Gamma\}\cup\{\langle\textbf{{L}},x\rangle,\langle\textbf{{L}},y\rangle\}
obtained by the

\epsilon
-concatenation of
\mathsf{LenTag}_{x}(A_{x})
and
\mathsf{LenTag}_{y}(A_{y})
, i.e.,

A_{\mathbin{\circ}}=\mathsf{LenTag}_{x}(A_{x})\mathbin{\mathbin{\circ}_{\epsilon}}\mathsf{LenTag}_{y}(A_{y})
.
The tags
S
are used for tracking the currently read symbol and

L
-tags are used for counting of the length of a word from the language of the corresponding variable.
Then
A^{\mathrm{I}}=(Q_{1}\cup Q_{2}\cup Q_{3},\Delta,I,F)
is a TA
over
\mathbb{T}^{\mathrm{I}}=\mathbb{T}_{\mathbin{\circ}}\cup\{\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},a\rangle,\langle\textbf{{M}}_{2},a\rangle\mid a\in\Gamma\}\cup\{\langle\textbf{{P}},x\rangle,\langle\textbf{{P}},y\rangle\}
, where
the
\textbf{{M}}_{1}
and
\textbf{{M}}_{2}

tags denote the first and the second
M
ismatch respectively and
\langle\textbf{{P}},x\rangle,\langle\textbf{{P}},y\rangle
are used to count the
P
ositions of the mismatch in
x
and
y
.

Note that in
\Delta
, the
\textbf{{M}}_{1}
-tagged transitions denote the occurrence of the
first mismatch (which causes a jump from
Q_{1}
to
Q_{2}
) and the
\textbf{{M}}_{2}
-tagged
transitions denote the occurrence of the second mismatch (jumping
from
Q_{2}
to
Q_{3}
).
For accepting runs of
A^{\mathrm{I}}
, it holds that they either

(i)

stay in
Q_{1}
and accept in some state from
F_{\circ}\times\{1\}
(so
we only keep track of the lengths of the words
w_{x}\in L_{x}
and
w_{y}\in L_{y}
) or

(ii)

take a
\textbf{{M}}_{1}
-tagged transition to
Q_{2}
and then
a
\textbf{{M}}_{2}
-tagged transition to
Q_{3}
and accept in some state
from
F_{\circ}\times\{3\}
.

An accepting run of the tag automaton encodes an assignment of
x
and
y
to
words from
L_{x}
and
L_{y}
. An example of a constructed tag automaton
is given in

5.1.2.
Formula Construction

After
A^{\mathrm{I}}
is constructed, it remains to test whether
there is a run of
A^{\mathrm{I}}
starting in
I
and ending
in
F
such that the number of occurrences of
\langle\textbf{{L}},x\rangle
and
\langle\textbf{{L}},y\rangle
differs
(corresponding to the case
|x|\neq|y|
), or the number of occurrences of the
\langle\textbf{{P}},x\rangle
and
\langle\textbf{{P}},y\rangle
tags is the same and there is one occurrence of a
\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},a\rangle
tag and
one occurrence of a
\langle\textbf{{M}}_{2},b\rangle
tag with
a\neq b
.
The means to this is via the Parikh tag formula
of
A^{\mathrm{I}}
.
First, we define formulae
\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\mathrm{I}}

and
\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{\mathrm{I}}
, which express
that the two sampled symbols are a mismatch and that there was a mismatch:

(4)

\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\mathrm{I}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\bigwedge_{a\in\Gamma}\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},a\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{2},a\rangle}<2\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{\mathrm{I}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\sum_{a\in\Gamma}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},a\rangle}>0.

In the formula, the first sum is used to check that the mismatched symbols are
indeed different (from the construction of
A^{\mathrm{I}}
,
there will be at most one
\textbf{{M}}_{1}
and one
\textbf{{M}}_{2}
tags in every
accepting run) and the second sum makes sure that there was at least one
mismatch (so that we can only accept in
Q_{3}
).
Finally, we construct the formula
\varphi^{\mathrm{I}}
equisatisfiable to
the disequality
x\neq y
as follows:

(5)

\varphi^{\mathrm{I}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A^{\mathrm{I}})\land\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x\rangle}\neq{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y\rangle}\lor\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}},x\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}},y\rangle}\land\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\mathrm{I}}\land\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{\mathrm{I}}\right)\right).

Theorem 5.1.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land x\neq y
is equisatisfiable to the formula

\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathrm{I}}
.
Moreover, the size of
\varphi^{\mathrm{I}}
is polynomial to
|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
.

5.2.
II: A Single Unrestricted Disequality

Let us now move to the case of an arbitrary disequality between concatenations
of (potentially repeating) variables:

(6)

x_{1}\ldots x_{n}\neq y_{1}\ldots y_{m}.\vskip-2.84526pt

This complex disequality is satisfiable if there are words
w_{x_{i}}\in L_{x_{i}}
and
w_{y_{j}}\in L_{y_{j}}
for all
i,j

such that either

(i)

both sides have different lengths (given by
\sum_{1\leq i\leq n}|w_{x_{i}}|
and
\sum_{1\leq j\leq m}|w_{y_{j}}|
respectively) or

(ii)

they are of the same length and there is a
mismatch
position

\ell
s.t.
w_{x}[\ell]\neq w_{y}[\ell]
where
w_{x}=w_{x_{1}}\cdots w_{x_{n}}

and
w_{y}=w_{y_{1}}\cdots w_{y_{m}}
.

We emphasize that there might be multiple occurrences of a single variable
z
,
potentially on both sides of the disequality, and they all need to be assigned
the same word from
L_{z}
.

We will again construct a tag automaton
A^{\mathrm{II}}
checking whether
one of the conditions to satisfy the disequality holds.
In this case, an accepting run in the tag automaton encodes an assignment
that maps every variable
z
from the disequality to a word from
L_{z}
.
The mismatch may happen in any pair of occurrences of variables

(x_{i},y_{j})
and, moreover, the variables might have multiple occurrences in the
disequality.
In the tag automaton, a run encoding a mismatch needs to nondeterministically guess
a pair of variables’ occurrences where the mismatch happens, the mismatch
positions within the variables, and the mismatch symbol itself.
In order to check that the guess is valid, we then construct a formula
that will use the Parikh tag image of
A^{\mathrm{II}}
and use it to check that

(i)

the mismatch symbols are different and

(ii)

the
global
positions of both mismatches are equal, meaning that
for a guess of mismatch variables
(x_{i},y_{j})
,
the mismatch position in
x_{i}
plus lengths of assignments of
x_{1}\cdots x_{i-1}
is equal to the
mismatch position in
y_{j}
plus lengths of assignments of
y_{1}\cdots y_{j-1}
.

Without loss of generality, we assume that the sets of states of

We also assume a fixed linear order on variables
\preccurlyeq

a unique concatenation of tag automata
for each variable.
First, for each variable

corresponding

.

5.2.2.
Formula Construction

For the satisfiability checking of the general disequality, we generalize the LIA reduction
from the previous section. As in the previous case, the LIA formula speaks about properties
of
A^{\mathrm{II}}
using the Parikh tag formula
\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A^{\mathrm{II}})
.

First, the formula expressing that lengths of both sides are different can be
defined as follows:

(7)

\varphi_{\mathit{len}}^{\mathrm{II}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\sum_{1\leq i\leq n}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{i}\rangle}\neq\sum_{1\leq j\leq m}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{j}\rangle}.

Next, for the case the lengths are the same but there is a mismatch, we begin by
defining a formula that checks that the particular mismatch symbols are
different (and that there is at least one mismatch) by generalizing the
formula
\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\mathrm{I}}
from the previous section:

(8)

\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\mathrm{II}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\bigwedge_{a\in\Gamma}\left(\sum_{x\in\mathbb{X}}\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},x,a\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{2},x,a\rangle}\right)<2\right)

In order to check whether the global mismatch positions on both sides are equal,
we need to make a case split ranging over all pairs
(x_{i},y_{j})
of occurrences of variables
from the left-hand side and the right-hand of the disequality.
For each such a pair, we define an auxiliary formula
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
comparing
global mismatch positions when the mismatch is between the two occurrences.

(1)

If
x_{i}
and
y_{j}
are occurrences of a different variable then:

•

if
x_{i}\prec y_{j}
,

(9)

\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},x_{i}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},y_{j}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle},

•

if
x_{i}\succ y_{j}
,

(10)

\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},x_{i}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},y_{j}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}.

The formulae express that the mismatch
position is given by the sum of lengths of preceding variable assignments and the local mismatch position in the particular variable
x_{i}
or
y_{j}
.

(2)

If
x_{i}
and
y_{j}
are occurrences of the same variable
z
, in order
to get the position of the second local mismatch we have to add

{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},z\rangle}
to
{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},z\rangle}
since the second
local mismatch in
z
has to be counted from the beginning of
z
and not
from the beginning of the previous mismatch.
Formally, the formula is given as

(11)

\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}

\displaystyle\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},z\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}\right)\lor{}

\displaystyle\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},z\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}\right).

Then, for each
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
, we need to combine it with a formula that
says that there are indeed mismatches in
x_{i}
and
y_{j}
, to obtain formulae

\varphi_{i,j}
as follows:

•

if
x_{i}\preccurlyeq y_{j}
(including the case when they are occurrences of the same variable),

(12)

\varphi_{i,j}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}\land\sum_{a\in\Gamma}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},x_{i},a\rangle}>0\land\sum_{a\in\Gamma}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{2},y_{j},a\rangle}>0,

•

if
x_{i}\succ y_{j}
,

(13)

\varphi_{i,j}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}\land\sum_{a\in\Gamma}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{1},y_{j},a\rangle}>0\land\sum_{a\in\Gamma}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{2},x_{i},a\rangle}>0.

We do the case split based on the order of variables since the construction
of
A^{\mathrm{I}}
guarantees in which variable will be which
mismatch.
All
\varphi_{i,j}
formulae are then collected into the formula

(14)

\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{\mathrm{II}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\bigvee_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq n\\
1\leq j\leq m\end{subarray}}\varphi_{i,j}

and the final formula equisatisfiable to
x_{1}\ldots x_{n}\neq y_{1}\ldots y_{m}
is
then defined as

(15)

\varphi^{\mathrm{II}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A^{\mathrm{II}})\land\Big(\varphi_{\mathit{len}}^{\mathrm{II}}\lor\big(\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\mathrm{II}}\land\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{\mathrm{II}}\big)\Big).

Theorem 5.2.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land x_{1}\ldots x_{n}\neq y_{1}\ldots y_{m}

is equisatisfiable to the formula

\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathrm{II}}
.
Moreover, the size of
\varphi^{\mathrm{II}}
is polynomial to
nm\cdot|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
.

5.3.
III: A System of Disequalities

We now move to the general case of a system of disequalities, which all need to
be satisfied at the same time:

(16)

\bigwedge_{1\leq i\leq n}L_{i}\neq R_{i}

where each
L_{i}
and
R_{i}
are arbitrary concatenations of variables, with
potentially multiple occurrences in multiple disequalities.
We, again, construct a tag automaton and a corresponding LIA formula for it.
The tag automaton for this case will be more complex.

One could extend the construction of
A^{\mathrm{II}}
from the previous
section in a straightforward manner by creating more copies of
A_{\circ}
.
With multiple disequalities, we need to keep track of satisfying position
mismatches in particular disequalities, so that we do not count two mismatches
in one disequality and zero mismatches in another disequality.
If done in a straightforward way, we would need to consider all possible orders
of mismatches in different disequalities, basically having one copy of the tag
automaton
A^{\mathrm{II}}
for each such an order.
The number of these copies and the size of the resulting automaton would,
however, be intractable.
In particular, if we consider a set of disequalities
D=\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{n}\}
,
we would need
\frac{(2n)!}{2^{n}}\in 2^{\Theta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n\log n}}\right)}
such copies
(obtained as the number of permutations of a set of
n
pairs of symbols

\textbf{{M}}_{1}^{i},\textbf{{M}}_{2}^{i}
, respecting the order
\textbf{{M}}_{1}^{i}\prec\textbf{{M}}_{2}^{i}
).

Another issue that we need to take into consideration is the fact that one
mismatched symbol may be used for solving more than one disequality.
For instance, for the system of disequalities
x\neq y\land x\neq z
and its
model
\{x\mapsto a,y\mapsto b,z\mapsto c\}
, the value of
x
is
a mismatch for both disequalities.
To deal with these issues, we take a more involved approach.
Our approach is based on introducing two new types of tags:

(i)

Instead of mismatch tags
\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i},a,x\rangle
for
i\in\{1,2\}

from
\mathbb{T}^{\mathrm{II}}
, we use more complex tags for mismatches of the
form
\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i},x,D,s,a\rangle
denoting that the
i
-th mismatched
symbol for the disequality
D
on the side
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\}
tracked for the variable
x
was
a
.
The mismatches can appear in an arbitrary order in an accepting run of the
tag automaton (potentially also multiple or zero times), so we will need to
extend the final LIA formula with a part that makes sure that we have
a mismatch for both sides of every disequality.

(ii)

We introduce
C
opy tags
\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i},x,D,s\rangle
, which express that the
i
-th mismatch symbol for disequality
D

and side
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\}
is given by the latest symbol
sampled by a
M
-tag for variable
x
.

With these two new kinds of tags and corresponding constraints added to the
final LIA formula, we suffice with having a tag automaton with only
2n+1

copies of
A_{\circ}
.

5.3.1.
Tag Automaton Construction

Let
A_{\circ}
be the
\epsilon
-concatenation of NFAs for all variables
obtained in the same way as described in
Sec.

5.2
.
Then
A^{\mathrm{III}}=(Q,\Delta,I,F)
is a TA
over
\mathbb{T}^{\mathrm{III}}=\mathbb{T}_{\mathbin{\circ}}\cup\{\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i},x,D,s,a\rangle,\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i},x,D,s\rangle\mid a\in\Gamma,x\in\mathbb{X},1\leq i\leq 2n,1\leq D\leq n,s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\}\}\cup\{\langle\textbf{{P}}_{i},x\rangle\mid x\in\mathbb{X},1\leq i\leq 2n+1\}
.

A^{\mathrm{III}}
is constructed as follows:

•

Q=\{(q,i)\mid q\in Q_{\mathbin{\circ}},1\leq i\leq 2n+1\}
,

•

I=I_{\mathbin{\circ}}\times\{1\}
,

•

F=F_{\mathbin{\circ}}\times\{1,3,\dots,2n+1\}
, and

•

\Delta
is the union of the following sets of transitions:

–

.

A run of
A^{\mathrm{III}}
nondeterministically guesses possible mismatches for
disequalities, as well as which mismatch is shared by multiple disequalities (the
correctness of the guess is enforced by the final LIA formula).
The run also guesses which disequalities are satisfied due to a mismatch and
which are satisfied by the lengths violation (that is why
F
contains
accepting states within all odd-labelled internal copies: each length-satisfied
disequality removes the need for two mismatches).
An example of a selected run of
A^{\mathrm{III}}
is shown in

Fig.

.

5.3.2.
Formula Construction

We construct a LIA formula equisatisfiable to the system of disequalities
based on the tag automaton described above.
Contrary to the case of a single
disequality, the resulting formula is enhanced by subformulae ensuring
consistency of each nondeterministic choice. For simplicity, we introduce auxiliary
(integer) variables describing particular choices that are then used in the LIA
subformulae:

(i)

m_{D,s}
variables containing the mismatch symbol for a disequality
D
and its side
s
and

(ii)

c_{i}
variables containing the shared
i
-th mismatch symbol (the mismatch symbol
preceding the
\textbf{{C}}_{i}
-tag).

We start with auxiliary subformulae expressing that the mismatches are consistent, meaning
that each disequality and side has at most one sampled mismatch and that these mismatches are
sampled consistently for both sides.
The first subformula
\varphi_{\mathit{Fair}}
checks that there is at most one mismatch for each side of each disequality:

(17)

\varphi_{\mathit{Fair}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\bigwedge_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}\\
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\}\end{subarray}}\Big(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq 2n\\
x\in\mathbb{X},a\in\Gamma\end{subarray}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i},x,D,s,a\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i},x,D,s\rangle}\leq 1\Big).

The subformula
\varphi_{\mathit{Consistent}}
then ensures that the quantified variables containing the mismatch symbols
are properly set, including the case of the copy tag, where the mismatch is
inherited from the previous mismatch transition.

(18)

\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathit{Consistent}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}{}\bigwedge_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}\\
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\},a\in\Gamma,\\
1\leq i\leq 2n\end{subarray}}

\displaystyle\bigg(\Big(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathbb{X}\end{subarray}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i},x,D,s,a\rangle}=1\Big)\rightarrow c_{i}=m_{D,s}=a\bigg)\land{}

\displaystyle\bigg(\Big(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathbb{X}\end{subarray}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i},x,D,s\rangle}=1\Big)\rightarrow c_{i}=m_{D,s}=c_{i-1}\bigg).

Since not all disequalities have to be satisfied by the existence of
a mismatch (but possibly also by a length violation), the values of
m_{D,s}

and
c_{i}
variables for disequalities with a missing mismatch (one side or
both) might hold arbitrary values.
Therefore,
it is not sufficient to compare only values of
m_{D,\mathcal{L}}
and

m_{D,\mathcal{R}}
but it is necessary to take into account existing
mismatches.
It remains to check the consistency of copy tags.
In particular, we need to ensure that copy tags for a variable
x
occur on
a run only if the previous mismatch or copy transition for
x
was taken.
We also need to check that a
C
-transition was taken immediately after
the previous mismatch or copy transition (
M
or
C
).

(19)

\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathit{Copies}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\hskip-5.69054pt\bigwedge_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq 2n\\
x\in\mathbb{X}\end{subarray}}

\displaystyle\bigg(\Big(\hskip 11.38109pt\sum_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}\\
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\},a\in\Gamma\end{subarray}}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i},x,D,s,a\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i},x,D,s\rangle}=0\Big)\rightarrow\Big(\sum_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}\\
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\}\end{subarray}}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i+1},x,D,s\rangle}=0\Big)\bigg)\land{}

\displaystyle\bigwedge_{\begin{subarray}{c}2\leq i\leq 2n\\
x\in\mathbb{X}\end{subarray}}

\displaystyle\bigg(\Big(\hskip 11.38109pt\sum_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}\\
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\}\end{subarray}}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{C}}_{i},x,D,s\rangle}=1\Big)\rightarrow{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{i},x\rangle}-\sum_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in\{D_{1},\dots,D_{n}\}\\
s\in\{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R}\},a\in\Gamma\end{subarray}}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{M}}_{i-1},x,D,s,a\rangle}=0\bigg).

We note that the last expression in
\varphi_{\mathit{Copies}}
,
{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{i},x\rangle}-\sum\ldots

, is there since we need to make sure that if there is
a
\textbf{{C}}_{i}
-tag immediately after an
\textbf{{M}}_{i-1}
-tag, the number
of
\langle\textbf{{P}}_{i},x\rangle
is one (because there was already one

\textbf{{P}}_{i}
tag on the
\textbf{{M}}_{i-1}
-transition),
but if a copy tag follows another copy tag, then the number of corresponding
position tags is zero.

The final formula will be

(20)

\varphi^{\mathrm{III}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A^{\mathrm{III}})\land\varphi_{\mathit{Fair}}\land\varphi_{\mathit{Consistent}}\land\varphi_{\mathit{Copies}}\land\bigwedge_{\mathclap{D\in\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{n}\}}}\big(\varphi_{\mathit{len}}^{D}\lor(\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{D}\land\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{D})\big),

where
\varphi_{\mathit{len}}^{D}
,
\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{D}
, and
\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{D}
are similar
to their counterparts in
Sec.

5.2
but using the
m_{D,s}

variables instead of directly using
M
-tags.
Details are in
Appendix

C
.

Theorem 5.3.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land\bigwedge_{1\leq i\leq n}L_{i}\neq R_{i}

is equisatisfiable to the formula

\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathrm{III}}
.
Moreover, the size of
\varphi^{\mathrm{III}}
is polynomial
to
mn\cdot|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
where
m
is the maximum size of any
L_{i}

or
R_{i}
.

6.
Other Position Constraints

In this section, we show how the framework introduced in
Sec.

5
can
be extended for solving other considered position constraints.

6.1.
Length Constraints

For conjunctions
\bigwedge_{1\leq i\leq n}x_{i}=\mathit{len}(y_{i1}\cdots y_{im_{i}})
, where
x_{i}
are integer variables, we create the

\epsilon
-concatenation
A_{\circ}
for all string variables occurring in the constraint and
construct the formula

(21)

\varphi^{\mathit{LEN}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A_{\circ})\land\bigwedge_{1\leq i\leq n}\Big(x_{i}=\sum_{\mathclap{1\leq j\leq m_{i}}}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{ij}\rangle}\Big).

Theorem 6.1.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land\bigwedge_{1\leq i\leq n}x_{i}=\mathit{len}(y_{i1}\cdots y_{im_{i}})

is equisatisfiable to the formula

\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathit{LEN}}
and
the size of
\varphi^{\mathit{LEN}}
is polynomial to
mn\cdot|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
.

6.2.
Not Prefix and Not Suffix Predicates

The
\neg\mathit{prefixof}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n},y_{1}\cdots y_{m})
and
\neg\mathit{suffixof}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n},y_{1}\cdots y_{m})
predicates are similar to a disequality
x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\neq y_{1}\cdots y_{m}
in that they are satisfied if there is a mismatch at the
same global position between their first and second argument.
Both predicates, however, have slightly different
conditions than disequalities on satisfiability due to their sides having incompatible lengths—the
first argument (
x_{1}\cdots y_{n}
) must be strictly longer than the second argument (
y_{1}\cdots y_{m}
).
Therefore, the tag-automaton construction is the same as in the
case of a single unrestricted disequality given in
Sec.

5.2
.
Forming an equisatisfiable LIA formula also remains the same, save for small
differences.
The different condition on satisfiability by
x_{1}\cdots x_{n}
and
y_{1}\cdots y_{m}

having incompatible lengths requires replacing the corresponding subformula

\varphi_{\mathit{len}}^{\mathrm{II}}
by
\varphi^{*\mathrm{FIX}}_{\mathit{len}}
defined as

(22)

\varphi^{*\mathrm{FIX}}_{\mathit{len}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\sum_{1\leq i\leq n}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{i}\rangle}>\sum_{1\leq j\leq m}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{j}\rangle}.

Furthermore, the
\neg\mathit{suffixof}
predicate treats the mismatch position
differently than
\neg\mathit{prefixof}
. Instead of being satisfied by a mismatch on the
same global position starting from the beginning of its arguments, the
\neg\mathit{suffixof}

predicate counts the mismatch position from the end of its arguments. Therefore, we
also need to replace the
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
subformulae with
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}^{\mathrm{NS}}

asserting that the mismatch positions in both arguments are the same, using the
\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},x\rangle
-tags, which we already added into
A^{\mathrm{II}}
in
Sec.

5.2
. We define

\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}^{\mathrm{NS}}
as follows:

(1)

If
x_{i}
and
y_{j}
are occurrences of a different variable, then

(23)

\hskip-5.69054pt\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}^{\mathrm{NS}}\!\!\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\!\begin{cases}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},x_{i}\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},x_{i}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},y_{j}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}~\textrm{ if }x_{i}\prec y_{j},\\[5.69054pt]
{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},x_{i}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},y_{j}\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},y_{j}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}~\textrm{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

(2)

If
x_{i}
and
y_{j}
are occurrences of the same variable
z
, then

(24)

\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}^{\mathrm{NS}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}{}

\displaystyle\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},z\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}\right)\lor{}

\displaystyle\left({\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq u<i}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{u}\rangle}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},z\rangle}+{\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{3},z\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq v<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{v}\rangle}\right).

Intuitively, we start counting the mismatch position inside a variable
after
the
mismatch has been sampled rather than counting
until
it has been sampled.
We denote the corresponding constructed formulae as
\varphi^{\mathit{pre}}

(for
\neg\mathit{prefixof}
) and
\varphi^{\mathit{suf}}
(for
\neg\mathit{suffixof}
).

Theorem 6.2.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land\neg\mathit{prefixof}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n},y_{1}\cdots y_{m})
is equisatisfiable to the formula
\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathit{pre}}
and the formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land\neg\mathit{suffixof}(x_{1}\cdots x_{n},y_{1}\cdots y_{m})
is equisatisfiable to the formula

\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathit{suf}}
.
The sizes of
\varphi^{\mathit{pre}}
and
\varphi^{\mathit{suf}}
are
polynomial to
mn\cdot|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
.

6.3.
Symbol (not) at a Position

Starting with the negative case first, let the input predicate be
x_{s}\neq\mathit{str.at}(y_{1}\cdots y_{m},x_{i})

where
x_{s},y_{1},\dots y_{n}
are string variables and
x_{i}
is an integer
variable. We construct the tag automaton
A
in the same way as described in

Sec.

5.2
. To form an equisatisfiable LIA formula, we
modify the reduction from
Sec.

5.2
to capture that
the mismatch position of the left-hand side is given by
x_{i}
rather than being
nondeterministically given by a run in the automaton:

(25)

\varphi_{1,j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\begin{cases}x_{i}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{1},y_{j}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq k<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{k}\rangle}&\text{ if }y_{i}\prec x_{s},\\
x_{i}={\#{}\langle\textbf{{P}}_{2},y_{j}\rangle}+\sum_{1\leq k<j}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{k}\rangle}&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

We further introduce an auxiliary predicate
\varphi_{\mathit{InBounds}}
checking that
x_{i}
is a valid position in
y_{1}\cdots y_{m}
:

(26)

\varphi_{\mathit{InBounds}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad 0\leq x_{i}<\sum_{1\leq j\leq m}{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},y_{j}\rangle}.

The final formula
\varphi^{\neg\mathit{str.at}}
is then modified to capture possible invalid positions of
x_{i}
:

(27)

\displaystyle\varphi^{\neg\mathit{str.at}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A)\land\bigg(

\displaystyle\big({\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{s}\rangle}>0\land\neg\varphi_{\mathit{InBounds}}\big)\lor{\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{s}\rangle}>1\lor{}

\displaystyle\big({\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{s}\rangle}=1\land\varphi_{\mathit{InBounds}}\land\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}\land\bigvee_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j\leq m\end{subarray}}\varphi_{1,j}\big)\bigg).

Theorem 6.3.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land x_{s}\neq\mathit{str.at}(y_{1}\cdots y_{m},x_{i})
is equisatisfiable to the formula
\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\neg\mathit{str.at}}

and the size of
\varphi^{\neg\mathit{str.at}}
is polynomial to
m\cdot|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
.

The
x_{s}=\mathit{str.at}(y_{1}\cdots y_{m},x_{i})
predicate can be reduced in a similar
fashion, requiring us to replace
\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}
with
\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\prime}
, which enforces
the sampled letters to be the same rather than being different.

(28)

\displaystyle\varphi^{\mathit{str.at}}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def.}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}\quad\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(A)\land\bigg(

\displaystyle\big({\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{s}\rangle}=0\land\neg\varphi_{\mathit{InBounds}}\big)\lor{}

\displaystyle\big({\#{}\langle\textbf{{L}},x_{s}\rangle}=1\land\varphi_{\mathit{InBounds}}\land\varphi_{\mathit{sym}}^{\prime}\land\bigvee_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j\leq m\end{subarray}}\varphi_{1,j}\big)\bigg).

Theorem 6.4.

The formula
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\land\mathcal{I}\land x_{s}=\mathit{str.at}(y_{1}\cdots y_{m},x_{i})
is equisatisfiable to the formula
\mathcal{I}\land\varphi^{\mathit{str.at}}

and the size of
\varphi^{\mathit{str.at}}
is polynomial to
m\cdot|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}|
.

6.4.
Not Contains Predicate

\bullet
offset
\kappa=3

v{:}

Figure 5
.

Demonstration of how
\neg\mathit{contains}(u,v)
for
u,v\in\mathbb{X}^{*}
is satisfied by an assignment
\sigma=\{u\mapsto aba
,
v\mapsto aabba\}
.
Symbols with
red
background present mismatches
in the corresponding alignments.

In this section, we extend the reasoning about the disequality tag
automaton
A^{\mathrm{II}}
introduced in
Sec.

5.2
to
handling
\neg\mathit{contains}
with flat languages.
The constraint
\neg\mathit{contains}(u,v)
for
u,v\in\mathbb{X}^{*}
is satisfiable
if there is a string assignment of variables from
u
and
v
yielding words
w_{u}
and
w_{v}
respectively such that
for
every
alignment of
w_{u}
and
w_{v}

(i)

there is a mismatch symbol of
w_{u}
and
w_{v}
or

(ii)

w_{u}
overflows
w_{v}
.

For example, considering the constraint
\neg\mathit{contains}(u,v)
, the assignment

\sigma=\{u\mapsto aba,v\mapsto aabba\}
is a model—for every
alignment of
aba
and
aabba
, there is either a mismatching symbol or a part
of
aba
is outside
aabba
(cf.
Fig.

5
).
The alignment of
w_{u}
and
w_{v}
can be characterized by the offset
\kappa\in\mathbb{N}
of
w_{u}
counted from the beginning of
w_{v}
.
Therefore, the semantics of
\neg\mathit{contains}
implicitly involves a universal
quantifier ranging over all possible offsets.

Since we need to consider mismatches for all offsets of
w_{u}
and
w_{v}
,
one might consider the formula
\varphi^{\mathrm{II}}
from

Sec.

5.2
, but changed such that the position constraints

\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
take into account a universally quantified offset
variable
\kappa
.
Such a solution, however, does not work, since we need that

(i)

for each value of
\kappa
, the string assignment remains the same (we
want to shift the same assignment to different positions given by the
offset and not obtain a different assignment for each offset), and

(ii)

for each offset the particular mismatch position and symbol (if any)
may be different.

The second property is problematic as the different offsets might involve
different runs in the tag automaton that are, however, over the same string
assignment.
For this reason, we need to impose a
flat language restriction
, since
for flat automata, the number of taken transitions (and so a model
of
\mathit{PF}(A)
) uniquely determines the accepted word.
On the other hand, for non-flat automata, this property does not hold.
E.g,. consider an NFA with a single state
q
(which is both initial and
accepting) and two transitions:
q\xrightarrow{a}q
and
q\xrightarrow{b}q
.
The two words
aabb
and
bbaa
accepted by the NFA are different, but they
have the same Parikh images.
Our restriction to flat languages gives us the guarantee that a model of the
Parikh formula uniquely determines the string assignment.

6.4.1.
Formula Construction

Let
\varphi=\neg\mathit{contains}(u,v)
where
u=u_{1}\dots u_{n}
and
v=v_{1}\dots v_{m}
are sequences of variables from
\mathbb{X}
such that

L(\mathsf{Aut}(x))
is flat for every
x\in\mathbb{X}
, and let
A^{\mathrm{II}}
be
a tag automaton constructed as described in
Sec.

5.2
.
Since we now need to speak about different runs of
A^{\mathrm{II}}
, we
lift the definition of the Parikh tag image to
explicitly speak about the Parikh variables, i.e.,
\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}(T,\#)

where
\#
denotes the set of all
\#
-prefixed variables
in
\mathit{PF}_{\mathit{tag}}
.
Since we need to speak about alignments of assignments, we also refine the
formulae
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
from
Sec.

5.2
to

\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}(\kappa,\#)
, explicitly relating the used Parikh variables
and the particular offset
\kappa
.
The offset
\kappa
is added to the left-hand side of every equation occurring
inside
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
, in order to express that the assignments of the
left-hand side are shifted to the right by
\kappa
.
The formula
\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}^{\mathrm{II}}
from
Sec.

5.2
is
then also changed into
\varphi_{\mathit{mis}}(\kappa,\#)
, which
uses
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}(\kappa,\#)
instead of
\varphi_{\mathit{pos}(i,j)}
.
